name: Straw drinking for coffee

lead: This habit means drinking coffee or other dark drinks through a straw so less liquid reaches the visible surfaces of the teeth, keeping them from yellowing over time. Whitening and appearance communities discuss it as a low-effort preventive habit.

Dental references list frequent consumption of coffee, tea, red wine and cola as causes of extrinsic stain, linked to tannins and other pigments. The idea is reduced contact time between pigmented drink and the front teeth. No study of straw use and staining was found.

paras: People use a reusable or paper straw with iced coffee, tea or other dark drinks and aim it toward the back of the mouth. It is a daily habit that costs nothing and sits alongside brushing and professional cleanings.
No harms are documented, and the effect on stain has not been measured.

angle.text: Whitening communities suggest sipping coffee or dark drinks through a straw so less liquid touches the front teeth and less stain builds up over time. It is a low-effort daily habit that protects a whitened smile. Its effect on stain has not been measured.

lead: Straw drinking for coffee is the habit of sipping coffee or other dark drinks through a straw so that less liquid touches the front teeth, in order to reduce visible staining. It is discussed in tooth-whitening and appearance communities as a low-effort preventive habit.

Dental references list frequent consumption of coffee, tea, red wine and cola as causes of extrinsic stain, linked to tannins and other pigments.[1][2] The same sources recommend identifying the cause of staining and note that most extrinsic stains are removed by cleaning.[1]
No studies of straw use and staining were found.
infobox: Reduce contact of coffee with front teeth

paras: Proponents use reusable or disposable straws with hot or iced coffee, arguing the drink bypasses the visible surfaces of the front teeth. How far liquid still contacts teeth during swallowing has not been measured in the sources reviewed.

Tannins in coffee and tea act as chromogens, and heavy consumption can stain enamel brown.[2] Extrinsic stains lie on the tooth surface; intrinsic stains form within it from causes such as ageing, trauma or fluorosis.[2] Treatment of extrinsic stain includes whitening toothpaste or professional scaling and polishing.[1] Staining is also affected by plaque and tobacco.[1]
